## Overview

::: {.callout-important}
## Focus for Today
This lab introduces **bootstrap confidence intervals** - a powerful resampling technique for estimating uncertainty:

- Understanding point estimates vs interval estimates
- Building confidence intervals through bootstrapping
- Interpreting what CIs tell us (and don't tell us)
- Connecting CIs to effect sizes
:::

---

## Activity 1: Understanding Point Estimates (15 min)

### The Problem with Single Numbers

When we calculate a mean from our sample, we get a **point estimate** - a single number. But how confident can we be in this number?


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](activity_files/figure-html/sample-means-demo-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


### Conceptual Questions

**1. A point estimate is:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>A single value calculated from sample data</option><option value=''>A range of plausible values</option><option value=''>The true population parameter</option><option value=''>A measure of variability</option></select>

**2. Why might a point estimate be misleading?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>It's always wrong</option><option value=''>It's too complicated</option><option value='answer'>It doesn't show how uncertain we are about the true value</option><option value=''>Point estimates can't be calculated</option></select>

**3. If we took a new sample of students and calculated the mean memory score, we would likely get:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Exactly the same mean</option><option value='answer'>A different mean due to sampling variability</option><option value=''>A smaller standard deviation</option><option value=''>The population mean</option></select>

True or False: The sample mean is always equal to the population mean. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>

## Activity 2: Building Bootstrap CIs (25 min)

### What is Bootstrapping?

Bootstrapping is a resampling technique where we:
1. Take our sample data
2. Resample WITH REPLACEMENT many times
3. Calculate the statistic of interest for each resample
4. Use the distribution of resampled statistics to estimate uncertainty

### The Bootstrap Process

**1. When we resample "with replacement", this means:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>We only use each data point once</option><option value='answer'>The same data point can be selected multiple times</option><option value=''>We add new data points</option><option value=''>We remove outliers</option></select>

**2. If our original sample has 30 observations, each bootstrap sample will have:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>More than 30 observations</option><option value=''>Fewer than 30 observations</option><option value='answer'>Exactly 30 observations</option><option value=''>A random number of observations</option></select>

**3. A typical bootstrap analysis might create how many resampled datasets?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>5</option><option value=''>50</option><option value='answer'>1000 or more</option><option value=''>It doesn't matter</option></select>

### Building a 95% CI

After creating many bootstrap samples and calculating the mean of each, we order these means and find the middle 95%.

**4. A 95% confidence interval uses which percentiles of the bootstrap distribution?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>0th and 100th</option><option value=''>1st and 99th</option><option value='answer'>2.5th and 97.5th</option><option value=''>5th and 95th</option></select>

**5. If our bootstrap means range from 5.2 to 7.8, and our 95% CI is [5.5, 7.3], this means:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>All bootstrap means fell in this range</option><option value='answer'>95% of bootstrap means fell in this range</option><option value=''>The true mean is definitely in this range</option><option value=''>Only 5% of bootstrap means fell in this range</option></select>

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Understanding the Bootstrap
The bootstrap works because our sample is our best estimate of the population. By resampling from our sample, we simulate what would happen if we took many samples from the population.
:::

## Activity 3: Interpreting CIs (20 min)

### What Does a 95% CI Mean?

This is one of the most commonly misunderstood concepts in statistics!

**1. The correct interpretation of a 95% CI is:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>There is a 95% chance the true mean is in this interval</option><option value='answer'>If we repeated this procedure many times, 95% of the intervals would contain the true mean</option><option value=''>95% of the sample data falls in this interval</option><option value=''>We are 95% certain of our results</option></select>

**2. True or False: A 95% CI tells us the probability that the true mean is in the interval.**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>

**3. A narrower confidence interval indicates:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>More precision in our estimate</option><option value=''>Less precision in our estimate</option><option value=''>A larger sample size only</option><option value=''>The true mean is closer to zero</option></select>

### Comparing Groups with CIs

When comparing two groups (like Lab A vs Lab B), we can look at whether their CIs overlap.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](activity_files/figure-html/ci-comparison-demo-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


**4. Looking at the plot above, do the CIs overlap?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Yes, they overlap completely</option><option value=''>Yes, they overlap slightly</option><option value='answer'>No, they do not overlap</option><option value=''>Can't tell from the plot</option></select>

**5. Non-overlapping 95% CIs suggest:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>No difference between groups</option><option value='answer'>A likely significant difference between groups</option><option value=''>The data is wrong</option><option value=''>We need more participants</option></select>

**6. If two 95% CIs overlap slightly, the difference between groups is:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Definitely significant</option><option value=''>Definitely not significant</option><option value='answer'>Uncertain - we need a formal test</option><option value=''>Impossible to determine</option></select>

## Activity 4: Effect Sizes (20 min)

### Beyond Statistical Significance

Confidence intervals tell us about precision, but **effect sizes** tell us about the magnitude of differences.

### Cohen's d

Cohen's d expresses a difference in standard deviation units:

$$d = \frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{SD_{pooled}}$$

**1. Cohen's d tells us:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Whether a result is statistically significant</option><option value='answer'>How large the difference is in standardised units</option><option value=''>The probability of the null hypothesis</option><option value=''>The sample size needed</option></select>

**2. According to Cohen's conventions, a d = 0.2 is considered:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Small</option><option value=''>Medium</option><option value=''>Large</option><option value=''>Negligible</option></select>

**3. A d = 0.8 would be considered:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Small</option><option value=''>Medium</option><option value='answer'>Large</option><option value=''>Very small</option></select>

**4. If two groups differ by d = 0.5, this means the difference equals:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>0.5 points</option><option value=''>0.5 percent</option><option value='answer'>Half a standard deviation</option><option value=''>50% of the mean</option></select>

### Confidence Intervals for Effect Sizes

Just like means, effect sizes have uncertainty. We can calculate CIs for Cohen's d.

**5. If Cohen's d = 0.6 with 95% CI [0.2, 1.0], what can we conclude?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The effect is definitely large</option><option value=''>The effect is definitely medium</option><option value='answer'>The effect is likely real (CI doesn't include 0) but size uncertain</option><option value=''>The effect is not significant</option></select>

**6. If Cohen's d = 0.3 with 95% CI [-0.1, 0.7], what can we conclude?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The effect is definitely small</option><option value='answer'>We cannot rule out zero effect - more data needed</option><option value=''>The effect is large</option><option value=''>The experiment failed</option></select>

True or False: Effect sizes help us understand practical significance, not just statistical significance. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

True or False: A statistically significant result always means a large effect size. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>

---

## Summary

::: {.callout-important}
## Key Takeaways

**Point Estimates vs Interval Estimates:**
- Point estimates give a single value (e.g., sample mean)
- Interval estimates (CIs) show a range of plausible values

**Bootstrap Confidence Intervals:**
- Resample with replacement many times
- Calculate statistic for each resample
- Use the distribution to estimate uncertainty

**Interpreting 95% CIs:**
- If we repeated the procedure, 95% of intervals would contain the true value
- Non-overlapping CIs suggest significant differences
- Narrower CIs = more precision

**Effect Sizes:**
- Express differences in standardised units
- Cohen's d: small (0.2), medium (0.5), large (0.8)
- CIs for effect sizes show uncertainty about magnitude
:::
